newsitem.title: USA: Crosby, Stills & Nash may rock to Wall Street beat.
newsitem.headline: Crosby, Stills & Nash may rock to Wall Street beat.

text.p: As Crosby, Stills & Nash get set for induction into the Rock n' Roll Hall of Fame this spring, Wall Street may be counting on yet another chart-buster out of the 1960s rock and roll icons.

Talk has it that the successful American group, comprised of David Crosby, Stephen Stills and Graham Nash, could soon be dancing to the same beat as British rocker David Bowie, by issuing a bond offering of its own.
"They (Crosby, Stills & Nash) are investigating all sorts of financial opportunities," said Michael Jensen, publicist for the group, and president of Jensen Communications Inc.

When asked if the group had decided to move forward with their own bond offering, Jensen replied: "It's too premature. I do know that they have been approached, and that they are talking and looking, at all offers right now."

Last month, David Bowie, with the help of U.S. brokerage firm Fahnestock & Co. Inc., successfully issued the first-ever music royalties future receivables securitization in the U.S. asset-backed market.
The deal featured $55 million in securities from DJT Royalty Financing Co., backed by a catalogue of Bowie songs, compositions and copyrights.
The bonds were priced with a 7.90 percent coupon with an average life of approximately 10 years.

After the Bowie offering, Fahnestock's David Pullman, who created the asset class along with Bowie business manager Bill Zysblat of Rascof Zysblat Organisation, said he had more such deals lined up for the future.
Pullman was not immediately available for comment Wednesday.

On Tuesday, Crosby, Stills & Nash group manager Gerry Tolman announced the band's longtime affiliation with Atlantic Records had ended, allowing the group to explore a number of financial and new media opportunities.
"This move enables Crosby, Stills & Nash to take full advantage of their phenomenal ongoing success," Tolman said.

"There's a wealth of opportunity out there right now - not only in the traditional sense, but certainly within the investment community, which has recently shown strong interest in forming alliances with name acts that have a solid, commercial track record," Tolman added.

By freeing up its obligation with Atlantic, Tolman said, the band will have the opportunity to open the door to new recording and investment opportunities such as the recent deal Wall Street made with David Bowie.
